title: Sharpe Ratio
body:
The **Sharpe ratio** measures return per unit of risk, which is what makes two investments
comparable when one earns more and swings harder.

$$
S = \frac{E[R_p - R_f]}{\sigma_p}
$$

The numerator is the [[Excess Return]], the return above the [[Risk-Free Rate]],
since a return available with no risk should not be credited to the strategy. The denominator
is [[Volatility]].

```
daily mean excess return   0.032%
daily standard deviation   1.2%

daily Sharpe    0.00032 / 0.012 = 0.0267
annualised      0.0267 × √252   = 0.42
```

Both parts scale with time and they scale differently, the numerator with $n$ and the
denominator with $\sqrt{n}$, so the ratio itself scales by $\sqrt{n}$, which is the
[[Annualisation]] factor.

Being dimensionless makes the number comparable across assets and periods, which is the
property that gives it its role. Roughly, above 1 is considered good and above 2 is considered
excellent, with the caveat that the figure depends on the period chosen.

Its assumptions are what the dashboard's explanatory text exists to state. It treats volatility
as risk, so it penalises upside swings alongside downside ones. It assumes returns are roughly
symmetric, which market returns are not. And it rewards a strategy producing steady small gains
with a rare catastrophic loss, because the rare loss barely moves a standard deviation computed
over years, which is exactly the profile of a strategy that blows up.
